title: The teacher who answered with silence
hookLine: Bahva answers with silence; the fourth has no letter, and the week in one breath
carry: the silence after om is the fourth

cards: A student named Bashkali once asked his teacher, Bahva: sir, teach me Brahman. Bahva said nothing. Bashkali asked again.
Silence. A third time: please, teach me. And Bahva said: I am teaching you.
You don't understand. This self is silence. Shankara, the great teacher of Advaita, tells this story.
And the Mandukya's last verse says the same thing in its own way.

teach.b: Verse twelve: the fourth is amatra, without a letter. Beyond all dealings. The world comes to rest in it.
Auspicious. Not two. So om is the self.
The one who knows this enters the self by the self. That's the end of the Upanishad.
The fourth isn't a sound after m. It's the silence the whole syllable rises out of and falls back into. That's why teachers ask students to stay quiet after chanting om.
The silence isn't the end of the practice. It's the point.
It's also why some Hindus keep mauna, a vow of silence, for an hour, a day, sometimes far longer. Not to punish the tongue. To rest where words come from.
And notice that last line: you enter the self by the self. Not by going somewhere else. By being what you already are.
The week, in one breath. The gods hid from Death in om, which is all this. Indra looked in the water and turned back: the self isn't the body.
Deep sleep is bliss that wants nothing. After a hundred and one years, the knower behind it all: the fourth. A, u, m, and the silence with no letter.
Today, a life barely has a rest in it: alerts, noise, a podcast for every walk. Hindu practice keeps a place for silence on purpose, because many teachers say that's where the self is closest.
Next, three weeks on three paths: action, devotion and knowledge.

how: Hindu practitioners who chant om are often taught to rest in the silence after the syllable, which the Mandukya's twelfth verse identifies with the fourth, the self beyond waking, dream and deep sleep.

games.q: you've chanted a, u, m. what does the Mandukya say about the fourth?
o: it has no letter; it's the silence.
games.why: the fourth is without a letter: beyond dealings, the world at rest, auspicious, not two.

practice: Breathe out slowly, all the way, and at the bottom of the out-breath, before the next one begins, rest in the small pause that nobody made.
Let the in-breath come by itself, and each time the breath empties, meet the pause again, not stretching it, just noticing it; if a thought arrives, let it fade the way a sound does.
If you'd like, chant om once at the start and let it fall into that same pause.

wordCard.voice: The Mandukya Upanishad. Twelve verses: om is all this; the self has four quarters; a, u, m for three of them, and silence for the fourth.

orig.note: Sanskrit: amatra, without measure, without a letter; Mandukya 12's word for the fourth.

carryVoice: Your line: the silence after om is the fourth. Tomorrow, the first of three paths: work. Day two hundred fifty-nine, and the Upanishads, done.
